config.title: Type a permission matrix model

intro.title: Type a permission matrix model
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a type-safe permission matrix model using TypeScript. This model will define user roles and their allowed actions, such as 'read', 'write', or 'delete', for different resources. You'll learn to use TypeScript's key concepts, including type aliases, unions, and mapped types, to enforce strict rules and prevent invalid permissions. By the end, you'll have a reusable, type-checked system that ensures only valid role-action combinations are allowed in your application.
intro.usecase: Permission matrices are foundational in enterprise software where different user roles need controlled access to features. You'll see this pattern in admin dashboards where managers can edit data but analysts can only view reports, or in SaaS platforms where team members have different capabilities based on their subscription tier. As a developer, you'll implement these permission models to secure customer portals, internal tools, and content management systems, ensuring users only see and interact with what they're authorized to use.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript interface to define the structure of a permission matrix
Implement a type alias for permission levels using union types
Apply mapped types to create a permission matrix from user roles and resources
Initialize a permission matrix object with typed data
Manipulate the permission matrix by adding new roles and resources
Configure type guards to validate permission access at runtime
Integrate the permission matrix model into a simple access control function

steps.title: Import TypeScript type utilities
steps.instruction: Import the Record utility type from 'typescript'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the Record type from the 'typescript' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing a type utility
import { Partial } from 'typescript';
steps.seedCode: // Import the Record utility type from 'typescript'
steps.expectedOutcome: The Record utility type is imported and available for use in defining the permission matrix.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the Record utility type.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing Record from 'typescript'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import Record from 'typescript'.

steps.title: Define the UserRole type
steps.instruction: Create a UserRole type using TypeScript's string literal union syntax with values 'admin', 'editor', and 'viewer'.
steps.hint: Use the type keyword followed by the union of string literals separated by the pipe (|) symbol.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a string literal union type
type Status = 'active' | 'inactive' | 'pending';
steps.seedCode:
// Import the Record utility type from 'typescript'

// Create the UserRole type here
steps.expectedOutcome: A UserRole type is defined with the three allowed string values.
successCriteria: The UserRole type is defined using string literal union syntax with 'admin', 'editor', and 'viewer'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the correct syntax for string literal unions and include all three roles.
steps.feedbackWrong: The UserRole type isn't defined correctly. Check the syntax for string literal union types in TypeScript.

steps.title: Define the Resource type
steps.instruction: Create a Resource type using TypeScript's string literal union syntax with the values 'dashboard', 'users', 'settings', and 'reports'.
steps.hint: Use the same union type syntax you used for UserRole, but with different string literal values.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a string literal union type
type Status = 'pending' | 'active' | 'inactive';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a Resource type that can only be one of four specific string values, representing different resources in your permission matrix.
successCriteria: The Resource type is defined as a union of the four string literals: 'dashboard', 'users', 'settings', and 'reports'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your Resource type includes all four string literals: 'dashboard', 'users', 'settings', and 'reports'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. The Resource type should be a union of four specific string values.

steps.title: Define the Permission type
steps.instruction: Create a Permission type using TypeScript's string literal union syntax with values 'read', 'write', 'delete', and 'manage'.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword followed by the type name and the union of string literals separated by the pipe (|) symbol.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a string literal union type
type Status = 'active' | 'inactive' | 'pending';
steps.expectedOutcome: The Permission type is defined as a union of the four string literals.
successCriteria: A Permission type exists with the exact string literal values 'read', 'write', 'delete', and 'manage'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Ensure the Permission type includes all four string literals: 'read', 'write', 'delete', and 'manage'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Permission type is not correctly defined. It should be a union of the four specific string literals.

steps.title: Create the PermissionMatrix interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'PermissionMatrix' that uses Record<UserRole, Record<Resource, Permission[]>> to create a matrix structure.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the name and the Record utility type with the types you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a PermissionMatrix interface that maps each UserRole to a Record of Resources, each containing an array of Permissions.
successCriteria: The PermissionMatrix interface is defined with the correct nested Record structure using UserRole, Resource, and Permission types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your interface uses Record<UserRole, Record<Resource, Permission[]>> exactly as specified.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PermissionMatrix interface is not defined correctly. Check the structure and types used.

steps.title: Create a sample permission matrix object
steps.instruction: Create a constant named 'permissions' of type 'PermissionMatrix' and initialize it with sample data that includes at least one user role and one resource with a permission.
steps.hint: Use the 'const' keyword to declare the variable, specify its type as 'PermissionMatrix', and assign an object that matches the interface structure.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed constant 'permissions' is created with sample data that demonstrates the permission matrix structure.
successCriteria: The 'permissions' constant is declared with type 'PermissionMatrix' and contains at least one user role and one resource with a permission value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the constant, but check that it's properly typed as 'PermissionMatrix' and contains the required sample structure.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constant is missing or doesn't match the expected type and structure. Review the PermissionMatrix interface and create sample data accordingly.

steps.title: Create a function to check permissions
steps.instruction: Create a function named hasPermission that takes three parameters: userRole of type UserRole, resource of type Resource, and permission of type Permission, and returns a boolean.
steps.hint: Define the function with proper TypeScript parameter types and a return type annotation. You can use the existing types from earlier steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: A type-safe utility function that can check permissions based on the provided parameters.
successCriteria: The hasPermission function is defined with correct parameter types (UserRole, Resource, Permission) and returns a boolean.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but check the parameter types or return type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or has incorrect syntax. Ensure it takes three typed parameters and returns a boolean.

steps.title: Add type annotations to the function parameters
steps.instruction: Add explicit type annotations to the parameters of your hasPermission function: userRole should be typed as UserRole, resource should be typed as Resource, and permission should be typed as Permission.
steps.hint: Look at the function signature and add a colon followed by the appropriate type name after each parameter name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The hasPermission function will have properly typed parameters, enabling TypeScript to catch type errors when the function is called.
successCriteria: The hasPermission function parameters userRole, resource, and permission each have explicit type annotations (UserRole, Resource, Permission).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some type annotations, but check that all three parameters (userRole, resource, permission) have their respective types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function parameters still need type annotations. Add : UserRole after userRole, : Resource after resource, and : Permission after permission.

steps.title: Implement the permission check logic
steps.instruction: Implement the function body of hasPermission to check if the given permission exists in the permissions matrix for the specified role and resource.
steps.hint: Access the permissions matrix using the userRole and resource as keys, then check if the permission array includes the given permission.
steps.expectedOutcome: The hasPermission function will return true if the permission exists for the given role and resource, otherwise false.
successCriteria: The hasPermission function body correctly accesses the permissions matrix and checks array inclusion.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure to access the matrix with both keys and check if the permission is included in the array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The implementation doesn't match the expected logic. Review how to access nested properties and use array methods.

steps.instruction: Add three sample calls to the hasPermission function with different parameters to demonstrate how the permission matrix works.
steps.hint: Call the hasPermission function with different user roles, resources, and permissions. Use console.log to display the results.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see the permission check results logged to the console, demonstrating how the permission matrix model works with different inputs.
successCriteria: Three sample calls to hasPermission with different parameters are added, and each call uses console.log to display the result.
